draft.title: Kinship, Country and identity
card: a system that sets how each person is related to others, including family, community and the wider world. It also sets their duties and responsibilities to those people.
the land, waters, sky and living things that a people belong to. It is more than a place on a map. People are connected to Country spiritually, and it is cared for as a relative.
Many Aboriginal peoples see identity as coming from these connections. Who a person is depends on their kin and their Country, not only on their own choices or achievements.
Aboriginal spiritualities are not all the same. Each nation has its own Country, kinship rules and stories, so details differ from one people to another.
draft.remember: Kinship and Country shape who a person is and what they owe to others.

a.q: In Aboriginal spiritualities, what does kinship set for each person?
opts: Their relationships and responsibilities to others
Their rank in a nation's group of leaders
Their right to own a section of land
Their place in a list of ancestors only
a.why: Kinship sets how a person is related to others and what they owe them. The tempting option about owning land mixes up kinship with Country, which is a spiritual connection rather than ownership.
a.clue: Think about who a person is connected to and what they owe them.

b.q: Tom is a young man who is learning to care for his people's Country by following the duties his kin teach him. What does this best show?
opts: Identity is linked to both kinship and Country
Identity is chosen by each person alone
Country matters only as a source of food
Kinship matters only inside the immediate family
b.why: Tom's duties to Country come through his kin, so his identity depends on both. The option about food is tempting, but Country is also spiritual and cared for as a relative, so it is more than a resource.
b.clue: Look at where Tom's duties come from and what they are about.

a.best: Their relationships and responsibilities to others

b.best: Identity is linked to both kinship and Country

problems.detail: All three wrong options contain an absolute ('alone', 'only', 'only'), and the right option is the only one without one. A student can pick it by spotting the absolutes without knowing the idea.

The why calls Country 'a spiritual connection rather than ownership'. The card defines Country as the land, waters, sky and living things that people are connected to, not the connection itself. Saying it is not about ownership also oversimplifies: 'traditional owners' is a standard Australian term, and kinship often does set a person's rights and responsibilities to particular Country.

check.summary: The card and answers are sound. Question b's right option stands out because every wrong option uses 'only' or 'alone', and why (a) misdefines Country and oversimplifies ownership.

proposal.title: Kinship, Country and identity
card: a system that sets how each person is related to others, including family, community and the wider world. It also sets their duties to those people, and can set their responsibilities for particular Country.
the land, waters, sky and living things that a people belong to. It is more than a place on a map. People are connected to Country spiritually and often care for it as they would a relative.
Many Aboriginal peoples see identity as coming from these connections. Who a person is depends on their kin and their Country, not only on their own choices or achievements.
Aboriginal spiritualities are not all the same. Each nation has its own Country, kinship rules and stories, so details differ from one people to another.
proposal.remember: Kinship and Country shape who a person is and what they owe to others.

a.q: In Aboriginal spiritualities, what does kinship set for each person?
opts: Their relationships and responsibilities to others
Their rank in a nation's group of elected leaders
The friends and goals they choose for themselves
The stories their people tell about the stars
a.why: Kinship is a system that sets how a person is related to others and what they owe them. The option about friends and goals is tempting, but kinship is not something a person picks for themselves.
a.clue: Think about who a person is connected to and what they owe them.

b.q: Tom is learning to care for his people's Country by following the duties his kin teach him. What does this best show?
opts: His identity is tied to both his kin and his Country
Kinship sets his duties to family but not to land
Country is valued mainly as a source of food for him
Caring for Country is a hobby he chose for himself
b.why: Tom's duties to Country come through his kin, so both shape who he is. The option saying kinship covers family but not land is tempting, but kinship can set responsibilities for particular Country, as it does for Tom.
b.clue: Look at where Tom's duties come from and what they are about.
